## What changed

This PR adds three per-step histograms. Each batch is sampled by exactly one scheduler rank: attention TP rank 0 and attention CP rank 0 on the final PP stage. That is the same predicate the FPM publisher uses (`_is_forward_pass_metrics_rank()`). With `--enable-dp-attention`, each attention DP group runs its own batch and emits its own series under its `dp_rank` label.

- `sglang:forward_pass_duration_seconds`: device-measured time of the batch's own forward segments. When one batch launches several segments (e.g. speculative draft + verify), their times are added. Labels: `phase`, `prefill_tokens_bucket`, `decode_reqs_bucket`.
- `sglang:decode_step_latency_seconds`: the same measurement, limited to passes with decode requests. Labels: `phase` (`decode_only` / `mixed`), `co_scheduled_prefill_bucket`, `decode_reqs_bucket`.
- `sglang:schedule_to_result_latency_seconds`: wall time from the start of batch selection to the end of result processing. Under overlap it includes the next batch's selection and launch, so it measures an engine step, not forward time.

**Attribution under overlap.** `run_batch` stamps each batch with the `[begin, end)` range of device-timer segments it launched (`DeviceTimer.num_started`). Result processing claims exactly that range. `event_loop_overlap` launches n+1 before it processes n, and n+1's forward is never charged to n. A step is skipped if it launched no timed segment, or if one of its segments has not finished. The metric never waits on the device.

**Enabling.**
- `--enable-metrics` alone exports only `schedule_to_result_latency_seconds`, on unified, PP and PD-disaggregated schedulers.
- The two forward-pass series also need the device timer: `SGLANG_ENABLE_METRICS_DEVICE_TIMER=1` or `--enable-forward-pass-metrics`. Without either, they stay empty.

**Other changes.**
- Labels come from an O(1) count on the batch (`prefill_stats`, `decoding_reqs`). They never read `seq_lens_cpu`, which spec-v2 overlap can leave as `None`. A decode batch that DP attention runs as a 1-token extend counts as decode.
- `fpm_start_time` is stamped on every batch selection, at the cost of one `time.monotonic()` call. This includes the PD-disaggregation decode and prefill selectors and the PP disaggregated prefill loop.
- FPM behavior change: the FPM publisher now also requires `attn_cp_rank == 0`. Before, every CP rank of a DP group started a publisher on the same `{base}.{dp_rank}` endpoint.
- Docs: `docs/docs/references/production_metrics.mdx`. It covers how to read the metrics, rank and DP semantics, and PromQL examples.

**Known limits.**
- With `--pp-size`, the forward-pass value is the final stage's forward, not full-model latency.
- FPM (ZMQ) `wall_time` still drains the device timer in bulk. #38711 addresses FPM timing ownership.
- Tested on CPU only (see Validation).

## Why

The production symptom this targets is: decode requests are streaming normally, then a long prompt/prefill request joins the scheduler batch, and existing decode streams suddenly see a p99 inter-token latency / TPOT spike. Request-level TPOT and ITL metrics are useful for user-visible latency, but they aggregate over a whole request. They do not tell us whether the slow decode token was delayed specifically by a long prefill that was co-scheduled in the same scheduler/model forward pass.

In production, this commonly shows up with mixed traffic:

- A chat workload has many short streaming decode requests already running.
- A retrieval or agent request arrives with a very large prompt, for example a 32k-100k token context assembled from documents, tool traces, or conversation history.
- The scheduler admits that prefill alongside active decode work in a mixed batch.
- Users on unrelated decode streams observe one or more slow token intervals, but the completed-request TPOT metric only says those requests had a bad tail. It does not identify the interfering engine step.

The right diagnostic unit is the scheduler/model forward pass, not the completed request. This PR records the device-measured time of each forward pass. Separately, it records decode-step latency for passes that include decode requests, and a schedule-to-result interval that also covers scheduling and launch cost. The labels intentionally stay low-cardinality: phase, bucketed co-scheduled prefill token count, and bucketed decode request count.

With these metrics, operators can compare:

- decode-only p99, where no prefill work was co-scheduled;
- mixed prefill+decode p99;
- mixed p99 grouped by co-scheduled prefill token buckets such as `16k_64k` and `64k_plus`.

A practical production diagnosis becomes possible: if `sglang:decode_step_latency_seconds` p99 for `phase="mixed"` and `co_scheduled_prefill_bucket="16k_64k"` or `"64k_plus"` is repeatedly much higher than `phase="decode_only"`, long prefill co-scheduling is likely contributing to decode ITL/TPOT tails. That gives an actionable signal for tuning chunked prefill, mixed batching, prefill throttling, or prefill/decode disaggregation.

This metric is intentionally not a replacement for completed-request TPOT. It is a forward-pass-level interference signal. Speculative decoding, stream interval, and two-batch-overlap can make one forward pass only an approximation of one visible token interval, so the metric should be interpreted as an engine-step latency proxy.

## Validation

Updated to current main on 2026-11-01. Removed the obsolete PDMux configuration guard because upstream removed PDMux; retained the canonical rank predicate and updated scheduler test fixtures for current upstream attributes/invariant checks.

- CPU unit tests: `test_forward_pass_metrics.py` and `test_scheduler_metrics_collector.py`: **58 passed, 51 subtests passed**. The repository's CPU kernel stub is used; device timing tests use CPU fakes.
- Pre-commit hooks on the PR's changed files: passed.
- GPU execution, accuracy, and performance remain unverified; upstream CI authorization is still required. No accuracy or performance result is claimed.

## Relation to other PRs

No other open PR adds per-forward-pass Prometheus histograms or a breakdown of decode interference. I searched open and closed PRs for "forward pass metrics", "decode step latency", "interference metrics", "schedule_to_result" and "device timer metrics". Overlapping PRs:
- #38711 (open) fixes FPM (ZMQ) timing ownership for speculative decoding through a `DeviceTimer` observer API. It serves a different consumer, but both PRs touch `DeviceTimer` and `_init_fpm`. If it lands first, I'll move these series to its API instead of `num_started`.
- #31319, #36387 and #39537 (open) fix the FPM request builder's `seq_lens_cpu is None` crash. This PR intentionally does not touch that builder; its series count labels from the batch instead.
- #29854 (mine, open) is a docs-only change to the same `production_metrics.mdx`. Its content is independent of this PR.

## Supporting data point: forward-pass granularity is also what engine-stall forensics needs

A recent production incident we root-caused (on vLLM, but the lesson is
engine-agnostic: vllm-project/vllm#37729,
[trigger analysis](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/37729#issuecomment-5018012967))
is a strong argument for exactly the framing this PR takes — that the
scheduler/model forward pass, not the completed request, is the right unit of
observation.

**The incident**: a flashinfer <= 0.6.13 Blackwell GDN prefill kernel hangs
permanently depending on **batch composition** — a forward pass whose varlen
batch had >= 5 rows with any row length not a multiple of 128 could wedge the
engine forever. No request-level metric could have localized this: the failure
was a property of which prefills the scheduler co-scheduled into one pass, not
of any individual request. We only found the trigger by instrumenting per-pass
batch shapes — effectively hand-rolling a crude version of what this PR
provides as standing metrics.

**Second, the detection angle.** During the wedge, every aggregate signal
failed in practice: the health endpoint stayed 200, and in one captured wedge
the running-requests gauge read 0 because the hang landed before the gauge
update, so gauge-based alerting misclassified a dead engine as idle.
Per-forward-pass metrics give the cleanest liveness signal we know of:
`rate(forward_pass_duration_seconds_count) == 0` while work exists cannot be
faked by a stale gauge.

One caveat worth designing for: a *hung* pass never completes, so the histogram
observation never fires — the stall is visible only as an absence of samples. A
tiny extension would make it a positive signal: also count pass *starts* (or
expose a last-pass-started timestamp). Then `started - completed > 0` sustained
for N seconds is an unambiguous mid-pass stall signature, distinguishable from
"no traffic" without reference to any gauge. That is precisely the signal our
incident needed and none of the existing metrics provided.

Happy to share the batch-shape instrumentation or the incident's forensic data
if useful as a validation scenario.

@RichardoMrMu thank you for the careful read, and sorry for the slow reply. Both points are correct, and together they say the metric as written does not measure what its name claims. Let me take them in turn.

**Overlap ordering — the interval includes n+1's work.** You're right. `fpm_start_time` is captured before timeout handling and batch construction, while the endpoint runs only after result synchronization, and `event_loop_overlap` selects batch n+1 before processing n and on the normal branch launches it first as well (scheduler.py 1804-1841). So n's observed interval is not bounded by n's forward — while the pair stays overlapped it carries n+1's selection and launch. That makes the number wrong in the specific direction that matters here: the metric exists to attribute decode slowdown, and this construction folds scheduling work into what a reader will interpret as forward time, so it would mislead exactly during the incident it is meant to explain. Your `disable_overlap_for_batch` observation is a good confirmation — that branch has the selection delay but not the launch delay, which is precisely the asymmetry you'd expect if the interval is bounded by the wrong event.

I'd rather fix this than document it. Capturing an end timestamp at n's forward completion (or reusing the existing device timer, which already has the right boundary) gives a real per-forward interval. And I think your second suggestion is the more important half: the engine-step / result-availability interval is genuinely useful, it is just a different quantity, so it should be named and exported as its own metric rather than being conflated with forward time. I'll split the two and add the overlap-ordering test you asked for, since that ordering is exactly the thing that regressed silently here.

**PP gating — N stage samples per logical step.** Also right, and this one is worse in the queries than in the code. The observer runs wherever `current_scheduler_metrics_enabled` is true, which under default gating is `attn_tp_rank == 0` on *every* PP rank, while the existing FPM path explicitly gates to the final PP rank. So with `pp_size=N` one logical step contributes N stage-local samples, and the example queries then `sum by (le)` and drop `pp_rank`, mixing stages into a single p99 and inflating the count by a factor of N. Someone reading that panel gets a latency distribution that is a blend of partial-stage timings and a throughput number that is simply N times too high, with nothing on the dashboard hinting at it.

Matching FPM and gating to one canonical PP rank is the fix I'd prefer, since it keeps the metric's meaning ("one sample per logical step") consistent with the rest of the FPM family and keeps the documented queries honest without every example having to carry a `pp_rank` selector. If you'd rather have genuine per-stage visibility I can define it explicitly as a per-stage metric instead and fix the docs to select a canonical rank in every example — but I don't think it should stay as it is, where it is per-stage by accident and documented as if it weren't.

I'll push the changes for both and re-request your review. Thanks again — these were not cosmetic, and the PR is better for the delay.

@RichardoMrMu both findings are now fixed, and the branch is rebased onto current `main`. Summary of what changed and the one decision I'd like your call on.

**1. Overlap ordering — the forward series are no longer wall-clock measured.**

You were right that no monotonic endpoint can work here. I tried to find one and there isn't: `run_batch` returns after launch, and the only later CPU-visible point (`copy_done.synchronize()` during result processing) is reached *after* n+1 has already been selected and, on the steady-state branch, launched. Any wall interval ending there is bounded by the event loop, not by the forward.

So the forward series now come from the existing forward `DeviceTimer` — your first suggestion — which brackets `model_runner.forward` / cuda-graph replay. That interval cannot contain n+1's selection or launch on either branch.

**2. The engine-step quantity is kept, but under its own name.** What the metric measured before is genuinely useful, so it is now `sglang:schedule_to_result_latency_seconds`, documented explicitly as spanning the next batch's scheduling and launch under overlap. The two forward series (`forward_pass_duration_seconds`, `decode_step_latency_seconds`) are device-measured. Splitting them means neither name lies.

**3. PP gating** now matches FPM exactly — `attn_tp_rank == 0 and pp_rank == pp_size - 1` — on both the emission and the timestamp stamp. `pp_size == 1` is unchanged. I checked the failure mode in the other direction too: `_pp_process_batch_result` is not rank-gated, so the final stage does reach `process_batch_result` and this does not swing from N samples to zero. The docs now also state that with `--pp-size` the value is the *final stage's* forward, not full-model latency — otherwise the number is easy to misread under PP.

**Tests.** The overlap-ordering regression test runs the same simulated step twice, with 0 ms and 50 ms of next-batch work after the forward, and asserts the forward observation stays 10 ms while only schedule-to-result grows. Reverting the production files makes it fail on the *value* (`0.020 != 0.010`), and three PP subcases fail `1 != 0` — so it regresses for the right reason rather than on a missing attribute. Also added tests that device time is not carried into the next batch, that the two series never leak into each other, and that the Prometheus drain still feeds FPM (`DeviceTimer._report()` fans out to all reporters; if that ever became single-subscriber FPM would silently read zero). Suite: 150 passed, 33 skipped in `test/registered/unit/observability/`.

**The decision I'd like your call on.** The device timer is only installed under `SGLANG_ENABLE_METRICS_DEVICE_TIMER=1` or `--enable-forward-pass-metrics`, so with plain `--enable-metrics` the two forward series now export nothing instead of a loop-bounded number. I chose that over auto-installing the timer on the `--enable-metrics` path, since that would add per-forward CUDA event timing to a default path and needs a non-CUDA-backend guard — a cost/behaviour decision that felt like yours rather than mine. `schedule_to_result_latency_seconds` still needs only `--enable-metrics`. If you'd prefer availability over that caution, say so and I'll wire the timer on. I'll update the PR description either way once it's settled.

First, a correction. My Sep 7 comment said both findings were fixed, but P1 was only partly fixed. The Sep 7 push moved the forward series onto the device timer, which kept n+1's selection and launch out. Result processing, however, still drained every completed timer segment. On the steady-state overlap branch n+1 is launched before n is processed. If n+1's forward had already finished on the device by then, n's sample took both forwards and n+1 recorded nothing.

### P1: overlap attribution ([thread](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/29879#discussion_r3872246547))

- `run_batch` reads a new `DeviceTimer.num_started` counter before and after the forward, and stamps the range on the batch as `forward_timer_span = (begin, end)`. The stamp runs after both `run_batch` branches. On the overlap branch, `forward_batch_generation`, and with it `DeviceTimer.wrap`, still runs synchronously inside that bracket.
- Result processing claims exactly the segments in that span and adds them up, because speculative decoding can launch several segments per batch. Segments launched later stay queued for their own batch. A step is skipped if it launched no timed segment, or if any of its segments has not finished. Nothing waits on the device.
- The engine-step interval is still exported separately as `sglang:schedule_to_result_latency_seconds`. Its docs say that under overlap it includes the next batch's selection and launch.
- Ordering test: `test_forward_duration_is_attributed_to_its_own_batch_in_every_loop` runs the real `Scheduler.event_loop_overlap` (both the steady-state and the `disable_overlap_for_batch` branch) and `event_loop_normal`. It goes through the real `run_batch` bracket and `ScheduleBatch.copy()`, and checks the launch/process order and forward durations of `[0.010, 0.030, 0.020]`. If I switch the claim back to the Sep 7 bulk drain, the overlap case gives `[0.040, 0.020]` and the other two cases still pass. One limit: the test runs `run_batch` with `enable_overlap=False`. For overlap, what it checks is the loop order; the stamp itself runs after both `run_batch` branches.
- Claim tests cover three cases: a sum over several segments, a span that is only partly finished, and a batch that went through `run_batch` without launching a timed segment. A separate test uses the real `DeviceTimer`, with `torch.cuda.Event` patched to run on CPU, and checks that `num_started` matches the ordinals of the reported segments.

Still open from Sep 7, and your call: the device timer is only installed with `SGLANG_ENABLE_METRICS_DEVICE_TIMER=1` or `--enable-forward-pass-metrics`. With plain `--enable-metrics`, only `schedule_to_result_latency_seconds` is exported and the two forward series stay empty. I haven't changed that. If you'd rather have them on by default, I'll wire the timer onto `--enable-metrics`.

### P2: one sample per batch ([thread](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/29879#discussion_r3872259944))

- The Prometheus series and the FPM publisher now use one predicate, `_is_forward_pass_metrics_rank()`: `attn_tp_rank == 0 and attn_cp_rank == 0 and pp_rank == pp_size - 1`. The Sep 7 push already matched FPM on TP and PP. The CP condition is new: with `attn_cp_size = K`, each CP rank was still emitting its own sample of the same batch.
- This also changes FPM behavior. Before, every CP rank of a DP group started a publisher on the same `{base}.{dp_rank}` endpoint. Now only CP rank 0 does. I'm pointing this out because it affects current FPM consumers on CP deployments.
- With `--enable-dp-attention`, each attention DP group runs its own batch and emits under its own `dp_rank` label. The docs now say so. The engine-step throughput query is now `sum by (dp_rank) (rate(sglang:schedule_to_result_latency_seconds_count[5m]))`. The `sum by (le)` latency queries are unchanged, because each sample now stands for exactly one batch.
- `test_forward_pass_metrics_emit_from_one_canonical_pp_rank` covers pp_size 1, 2 and 4, a non-zero attention TP rank, and a non-zero attention CP rank.

### Other changes since Sep 7

- `--enable-pdmux`: all three series are off there. Decode and split prefill share one timer under pdmux, so one batch's forward can't be separated out.
- PD disaggregation: `fpm_start_time` is now stamped in the disaggregated decode and prefill selectors and in the PP disaggregated prefill loop, so `schedule_to_result_latency_seconds` is sampled there too. `get_next_batch_to_run` now always stamps it (one `time.monotonic()` call per selection) and no longer reads the metrics reporter.
- Labels now come from an O(1) count on the batch. Before, they went through the FPM request builder, which walked `seq_lens_cpu` on every step and crashed on the `None` that spec-v2 overlap leaves there. A decode batch that DP attention runs as a 1-token extend now counts as decode. The docs note that under DP attention, a `decode_only` tail can come from prefill on another rank.
- I left the FPM request builder's `seq_lens_cpu is None` handling out of this PR on purpose. #31319, #36387 and #39537 already fix it, and these series no longer depend on it.
- Removed the unused import that failed ruff in the last CI run.

Related: #38711 fixes FPM (ZMQ) timing ownership through a `DeviceTimer` observer API. I didn't touch FPM timing here, so FPM `wall_time` on this branch still drains in bulk. If #38711 lands first, I'll move these series onto its API instead of keeping a second mechanism in `DeviceTimer`.

Thanks for adding these metrics. Reading `c30a6f0`, I think `decode_step_latency_seconds` doesn't see prefill stalls when `--enable-mixed-chunk` is off, which is the default.

`_forward_pass_composition` counts decode requests as `len(batch.decoding_reqs)`, and `decoding_reqs` is set only when `mix_with_running` merges the running batch into the prefill batch. Without mixed chunk, `get_next_batch_to_run` runs the prefill batch first and the running decode batch waits a whole step. That step is recorded as `forward_pass_duration_seconds{phase="prefill_only", decode_reqs_bucket="0"}` and never reaches `decode_step_latency_seconds`.

So the check in the docs (`mixed` p99 against `decode_only` p99) shows no interference while prefill is stalling streams. Mixed chunk is off by default on current `main`, and some configurations (diffusion LLMs, HiSparse, several speculative decoding setups) turn it off or reject it, so enabling it doesn't always work around this.

I measured this client-side with Qwen3-8B on one H100, SGLang v0.5.21, defaults (mixed chunk off, chunked prefill 8,192). The load was 8 short streaming requests/s, alone and then with one 3,118-token prompt per second added:

| | alone | with long prompts |
|---|---|---|
| inter-token gaps over 50 ms, per minute | 27 | 361 |
| replies with such a gap | 5% | 48% |
| p99 inter-token gap | 20 ms | 23 ms |
| p99.9 inter-token gap | 33 ms | 84 ms |
| longest gap | 108 ms | 255 ms |

724 of the 739 gaps over 30 ms began within 0.15 s of a long prompt arriving. Each long prompt fits in one 8,192-token chunk, so these gaps are prefill-only steps (one, or a few back to back) while the decode batch waits.

A possible fix: `prefill_stats` already carries `num_running_reqs` for the batch that waits. For an extend pass without `decoding_reqs`, record the pass in `decode_step_latency_seconds` under its own phase, e.g. `phase="prefill_blocking"`, with `decode_reqs_bucket` from that count. The docs would then compare `mixed|prefill_blocking` against `decode_only`. I'm happy to send this as a commit on your branch or as a follow-up PR, whichever you prefer.

@hirenp thanks, I checked `c30a6f0` and reproduced the omission in a CPU-only harness using the unmodified scheduler-selection and metrics method bodies, with model/CUDA dependencies faked.

With four running decode requests, a 3,118-token prefill and a synthetic 20 ms device-timer sample, the scheduler selects prefill and retains the decode batch. The sample reaches `forward_pass_duration_seconds{phase="prefill_only", decode_reqs_bucket="0"}`, but not `decode_step_latency_seconds`. Mixed and decode-only controls emit normally. All six focused checks passed; I haven't reproduced the H100 benchmark.

`prefill_blocking` makes sense for the decode-side series. I'd keep waiting-decode counts separate from scheduled-decode counts so the forward-pass series still describes the work actually executed. Here `num_running_reqs` is a `QueueCount` (`.total`), and the collector currently derives the decode phase from the prefill count, so that needs updating too.

Please send the change against this PR's branch. A regression covering prefill with and without waiting decodes, plus the updated PromQL, would be helpful. Thanks for offering to contribute.

detail.body:
## What changed

This PR adds three per-step histograms. Each batch is sampled by exactly one scheduler rank: attention TP rank 0 and attention CP rank 0 on the final PP stage. That is the same predicate the FPM publisher uses (`_is_forward_pass_metrics_rank()`). With `--enable-dp-attention`, each attention DP group runs its own batch and emits its own series under its `dp_rank` label.

- `sglang:forward_pass_duration_seconds`: device-measured time of the batch's own forward segments. When one batch launches several segments (e.g. speculative draft + verify), their times are added. Labels: `phase`, `prefill_tokens_bucket`, `decode_reqs_bucket`.
- `sglang:decode_step_latency_seconds`: the same measurement, limited to passes with decode requests. Labels: `phase` (`decode_only` / `mixed`), `co_scheduled_prefill_bucket`, `decode_reqs_bucket`.
- `sglang:schedule_to_result_latency_seconds`: wall time from the start of batch selection to the end of result processing. Under overlap it includes the next batch's selection and launch, so it measures an engine step, not forward time.

**Attribution under overlap.** `run_batch` stamps each batch with the `[begin, end)` range of device-timer segments it launched (`DeviceTimer.num_started`). Result processing claims exactly that range. `event_loop_overlap` launches n+1 before it processes n, and n+1's forward is never charged to n. A step is skipped if it launched no timed segment, or if one of its segments has not finished. The metric never waits on the device.

**Enabling.**
- `--enable-metrics` alone exports only `schedule_to_result_latency_seconds`, on unified, PP and PD-disaggregated schedulers.
- The two forward-pass series also need the device timer: `SGLANG_ENABLE_METRICS_DEVICE_TIMER=1` or `--enable-forward-pass-metrics`. Without either, they stay empty.

**Other changes.**
- Labels come from an O(1) count on the batch (`prefill_stats`, `decoding_reqs`). They never read `seq_lens_cpu`, which spec-v2 overlap can leave as `None`. A decode batch that DP attention runs as a 1-token extend counts as decode.
- `fpm_start_time` is stamped on every batch selection, at the cost of one `time.monotonic()` call. This includes the PD-disaggregation decode and prefill selectors and the PP disaggregated prefill loop.
- FPM behavior change: the FPM publisher now also requires `attn_cp_rank == 0`. Before, every CP rank of a DP group started a publisher on the same `{base}.{dp_rank}` endpoint.
- Docs: `docs/docs/references/production_metrics.mdx`. It covers how to read the metrics, rank and DP semantics, and PromQL examples.

**Known limits.**
- With `--pp-size`, the forward-pass value is the final stage's forward, not full-model latency.
- FPM (ZMQ) `wall_time` still drains the device timer in bulk. #38711 addresses FPM timing ownership.
- Tested on CPU only (see Validation).

## Why

The production symptom this targets is: decode requests are streaming normally, then a long prompt/prefill request joins the scheduler batch, and existing decode streams suddenly see a p99 inter-token latency / TPOT spike. Request-level TPOT and ITL metrics are useful for user-visible latency, but they aggregate over a whole request. They do not tell us whether the slow decode token was delayed specifically by a long prefill that was co-scheduled in the same scheduler/model forward pass.

In production, this commonly shows up with mixed traffic:

- A chat workload has many short streaming decode requests already running.
- A retrieval or agent request arrives with a very large prompt, for example a 32k-100k token context assembled from documents, tool traces, or conversation history.
- The scheduler admits that prefill alongside active decode work in a mixed batch.
- Users on unrelated decode streams observe one or more slow token intervals, but the completed-request TPOT metric only says those requests had a bad tail. It does not identify the interfering engine step.

The right diagnostic unit is the scheduler/model forward pass, not the completed request. This PR records the device-measured time of each forward pass. Separately, it records decode-step latency for passes that include decode requests, and a schedule-to-result interval that also covers scheduling and launch cost. The labels intentionally stay low-cardinality: phase, bucketed co-scheduled prefill token count, and bucketed decode request count.

With these metrics, operators can compare:

- decode-only p99, where no prefill work was co-scheduled;
- mixed prefill+decode p99;
- mixed p99 grouped by co-scheduled prefill token buckets such as `16k_64k` and `64k_plus`.

A practical production diagnosis becomes possible: if `sglang:decode_step_latency_seconds` p99 for `phase="mixed"` and `co_scheduled_prefill_bucket="16k_64k"` or `"64k_plus"` is repeatedly much higher than `phase="decode_only"`, long prefill co-scheduling is likely contributing to decode ITL/TPOT tails. That gives an actionable signal for tuning chunked prefill, mixed batching, prefill throttling, or prefill/decode disaggregation.

This metric is intentionally not a replacement for completed-request TPOT. It is a forward-pass-level interference signal. Speculative decoding, stream interval, and two-batch-overlap can make one forward pass only an approximation of one visible token interval, so the metric should be interpreted as an engine-step latency proxy.

## Validation

Updated to current main on 2026-11-01. Removed the obsolete PDMux configuration guard because upstream removed PDMux; retained the canonical rank predicate and updated scheduler test fixtures for current upstream attributes/invariant checks.

- CPU unit tests: `test_forward_pass_metrics.py` and `test_scheduler_metrics_collector.py`: **58 passed, 51 subtests passed**. The repository's CPU kernel stub is used; device timing tests use CPU fakes.
- Pre-commit hooks on the PR's changed files: passed.
- GPU execution, accuracy, and performance remain unverified; upstream CI authorization is still required. No accuracy or performance result is claimed.

## Relation to other PRs

No other open PR adds per-forward-pass Prometheus histograms or a breakdown of decode interference. I searched open and closed PRs for "forward pass metrics", "decode step latency", "interference metrics", "schedule_to_result" and "device timer metrics". Overlapping PRs:
- #38711 (open) fixes FPM (ZMQ) timing ownership for speculative decoding through a `DeviceTimer` observer API. It serves a different consumer, but both PRs touch `DeviceTimer` and `_init_fpm`. If it lands first, I'll move these series to its API instead of `num_started`.
- #31319, #36387 and #39537 (open) fix the FPM request builder's `seq_lens_cpu is None` crash. This PR intentionally does not touch that builder; its series count labels from the batch instead.
- #29854 (mine, open) is a docs-only change to the same `production_metrics.mdx`. Its content is independent of this PR.

+## Forward-Pass Decode Interference Metrics
+
+SGLang exports per-forward-pass histograms for diagnosing whether long prefill
+work co-scheduled with decode work is causing decode-step latency tail spikes.
+
+Two different quantities are exported, under names that keep them apart,
+because only one of them is forward time:
+
+- `sglang:forward_pass_duration_seconds`: Histogram of the duration of a single
+  model forward pass, as measured on the device. The `phase` label is
+  `prefill_only`, `decode_only`, `mixed`, or `other`. With `--pp-size` greater
+  than one the emitting rank is the final pipeline stage, so the value is that
+  stage's forward — a fraction of the full model's per-step device time, not
+  the end-to-end pipeline latency.
+- `sglang:decode_step_latency_seconds`: The same measurement restricted to
+  passes that include decode requests or that running decode requests waited
+  for. This approximates the delay active decoding requests experience before
+  the next decode step completes. Without `--enable-mixed-chunk` (the default),
+  a prefill pass runs alone while the running requests wait for it; that pass
+  is recorded here as `phase="prefill_blocking"`.
+- `sglang:schedule_to_result_latency_seconds`: Histogram of the wall-clock
+  interval from the start of a batch's scheduling decision to the end of its
+  result processing. Under overlap this span also covers the *next* batch's
+  scheduling and launch, so it is an engine-step pipeline latency and must not
+  be read as forward-pass time. It is the right series for "how long did one
+  scheduler iteration take end to end", and it is what shows a regression in
+  scheduling or launch cost that leaves the forward itself untouched.
+
+Labels:
+
+- `phase`: Scheduling phase derived from scheduled prefill token and decode
+  request counts. `sglang:decode_step_latency_seconds` uses `decode_only`,
+  `mixed`, and `prefill_blocking`.
+- `prefill_tokens_bucket`: Bucketed scheduled prefill token count for
+  `sglang:forward_pass_duration_seconds` and
+  `sglang:schedule_to_result_latency_seconds`.
+- `co_scheduled_prefill_bucket`: Bucketed scheduled prefill token count for
+  `sglang:decode_step_latency_seconds`.
+- `decode_reqs_bucket`: Bucketed number of scheduled decode requests. For
+  `phase="prefill_blocking"`, the number of unfinished running requests at
+  prefill selection.
+
+Prefill token buckets are `0`, `1_1k`, `1k_4k`, `4k_16k`, `16k_64k`, and
+`64k_plus`. Decode request buckets are `0`, `1`, `2_4`, `5_8`, `9_16`,
+`17_32`, and `33_plus`.
+
+With overlap scheduling, prefill selection can precede processing the previous
+decode result. A request that finishes in that in-flight result can therefore
+be counted in one prefill-blocking snapshot; later snapshots exclude it. The
+histogram records one device duration per prefill pass, not per-request
+inter-token latency.
+

+
+`sglang:schedule_to_result_latency_seconds` needs only `--enable-metrics`.
+
+The two forward-pass series additionally need the forward device timer, which
+is what gives them a boundary that is the forward pass itself rather than a
+position in the scheduler loop. Start the server with either
+`SGLANG_ENABLE_METRICS_DEVICE_TIMER=1` in the environment or
+`--enable-forward-pass-metrics`; without one of them those two series stay
+empty rather than reporting a scheduler-loop interval under a forward-pass
+name.
+
+Each batch is sampled by exactly one scheduler rank: attention TP rank 0 and
+attention CP rank 0 on the final pipeline stage, the same rank predicate the
+forward-pass metrics publisher uses. The other TP, CP and PP ranks run the same
+batch and export nothing, so the queries below can aggregate over `le` without
+a `tp_rank` or `pp_rank` selector; with `--pp-size` set, stages other than the
+last stay silent rather than adding N samples per step. This holds under
+`--enable-metrics-for-all-schedulers` too: that flag widens the other scheduler
+metrics to every rank, but these three stay on the one rank so that one sample
+still means one batch.
+
+With `--enable-dp-attention`, each attention DP group runs its own batch, so
+each group exports its own samples under its `dp_rank` label, and one engine
+step yields one sample per `dp_rank`.
+
+`sglang:schedule_to_result_latency_seconds` samples every engine step, on
+unified, pipeline-parallel and PD-disaggregated schedulers. A forward-pass
+sample is the device time of exactly the forward segments that batch's own
+launch recorded, summed when one batch launches several (for example
+speculative draft and verify). Under overlap the next batch's forward may
+already have finished when this batch's result is processed; it is left for
+the next batch's sample rather than folded into this one. A step is skipped
+only when it launched no timed forward segment (for example a
+disaggregated-decode placeholder batch), or, defensively, when one of its
+segments has not completed by result processing; the metric never waits on the
+device to find out.
+

+```bash
+curl http://localhost:<metrics_port>/metrics | grep -E "decode_step_latency|forward_pass_duration|schedule_to_result_latency"
+```

+
+These metrics are intentionally not completed-request TPOT. Speculative
+decoding, stream interval, and two-batch-overlap can make "one forward pass
+equals one visible token interval" only approximate.
+
+`sglang:schedule_to_result_latency_seconds` minus
+`sglang:forward_pass_duration_seconds` is the scheduler-side share of an engine
+step. A gap that widens while forward duration stays flat points at scheduling
+or launch cost, not at the model.
+
+With DP attention the attention DP ranks run each forward in lockstep, so a
+prefill on one rank can stretch a step that carries only decode requests on
+another. That step is recorded on the decode rank as `phase="decode_only"` with

+batch. A `decode_only` tail that tracks prefill on peer ranks is cross-rank
+interference, not a slow decode.

+  )

+```

+  0.99,

## Supporting data point: forward-pass granularity is also what engine-stall forensics needs

A recent production incident we root-caused (on vLLM, but the lesson is
engine-agnostic: vllm-project/vllm#37729,
[trigger analysis](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/37729#issuecomment-5018012967))
is a strong argument for exactly the framing this PR takes — that the
scheduler/model forward pass, not the completed request, is the right unit of
observation.

**The incident**: a flashinfer <= 0.6.13 Blackwell GDN prefill kernel hangs
permanently depending on **batch composition** — a forward pass whose varlen
batch had >= 5 rows with any row length not a multiple of 128 could wedge the
engine forever. No request-level metric could have localized this: the failure
was a property of which prefills the scheduler co-scheduled into one pass, not
of any individual request. We only found the trigger by instrumenting per-pass
batch shapes — effectively hand-rolling a crude version of what this PR
provides as standing metrics.

**Second, the detection angle.** During the wedge, every aggregate signal
failed in practice: the health endpoint stayed 200, and in one captured wedge
the running-requests gauge read 0 because the hang landed before the gauge
update, so gauge-based alerting misclassified a dead engine as idle.
Per-forward-pass metrics give the cleanest liveness signal we know of:
`rate(forward_pass_duration_seconds_count) == 0` while work exists cannot be
faked by a stale gauge.

One caveat worth designing for: a *hung* pass never completes, so the histogram
observation never fires — the stall is visible only as an absence of samples. A
tiny extension would make it a positive signal: also count pass *starts* (or
expose a last-pass-started timestamp). Then `started - completed > 0` sustained
for N seconds is an unambiguous mid-pass stall signature, distinguishable from
"no traffic" without reference to any gauge. That is precisely the signal our
incident needed and none of the existing metrics provided.

Happy to share the batch-shape instrumentation or the incident's forensic data
if useful as a validation scenario.

@RichardoMrMu thank you for the careful read, and sorry for the slow reply. Both points are correct, and together they say the metric as written does not measure what its name claims. Let me take them in turn.

**Overlap ordering — the interval includes n+1's work.** You're right. `fpm_start_time` is captured before timeout handling and batch construction, while the endpoint runs only after result synchronization, and `event_loop_overlap` selects batch n+1 before processing n and on the normal branch launches it first as well (scheduler.py 1804-1841). So n's observed interval is not bounded by n's forward — while the pair stays overlapped it carries n+1's selection and launch. That makes the number wrong in the specific direction that matters here: the metric exists to attribute decode slowdown, and this construction folds scheduling work into what a reader will interpret as forward time, so it would mislead exactly during the incident it is meant to explain. Your `disable_overlap_for_batch` observation is a good confirmation — that branch has the selection delay but not the launch delay, which is precisely the asymmetry you'd expect if the interval is bounded by the wrong event.

I'd rather fix this than document it. Capturing an end timestamp at n's forward completion (or reusing the existing device timer, which already has the right boundary) gives a real per-forward interval. And I think your second suggestion is the more important half: the engine-step / result-availability interval is genuinely useful, it is just a different quantity, so it should be named and exported as its own metric rather than being conflated with forward time. I'll split the two and add the overlap-ordering test you asked for, since that ordering is exactly the thing that regressed silently here.

**PP gating — N stage samples per logical step.** Also right, and this one is worse in the queries than in the code. The observer runs wherever `current_scheduler_metrics_enabled` is true, which under default gating is `attn_tp_rank == 0` on *every* PP rank, while the existing FPM path explicitly gates to the final PP rank. So with `pp_size=N` one logical step contributes N stage-local samples, and the example queries then `sum by (le)` and drop `pp_rank`, mixing stages into a single p99 and inflating the count by a factor of N. Someone reading that panel gets a latency distribution that is a blend of partial-stage timings and a throughput number that is simply N times too high, with nothing on the dashboard hinting at it.

Matching FPM and gating to one canonical PP rank is the fix I'd prefer, since it keeps the metric's meaning ("one sample per logical step") consistent with the rest of the FPM family and keeps the documented queries honest without every example having to carry a `pp_rank` selector. If you'd rather have genuine per-stage visibility I can define it explicitly as a per-stage metric instead and fix the docs to select a canonical rank in every example — but I don't think it should stay as it is, where it is per-stage by accident and documented as if it weren't.

I'll push the changes for both and re-request your review. Thanks again — these were not cosmetic, and the PR is better for the delay.

@RichardoMrMu both findings are now fixed, and the branch is rebased onto current `main`. Summary of what changed and the one decision I'd like your call on.

**1. Overlap ordering — the forward series are no longer wall-clock measured.**

You were right that no monotonic endpoint can work here. I tried to find one and there isn't: `run_batch` returns after launch, and the only later CPU-visible point (`copy_done.synchronize()` during result processing) is reached *after* n+1 has already been selected and, on the steady-state branch, launched. Any wall interval ending there is bounded by the event loop, not by the forward.

So the forward series now come from the existing forward `DeviceTimer` — your first suggestion — which brackets `model_runner.forward` / cuda-graph replay. That interval cannot contain n+1's selection or launch on either branch.

**2. The engine-step quantity is kept, but under its own name.** What the metric measured before is genuinely useful, so it is now `sglang:schedule_to_result_latency_seconds`, documented explicitly as spanning the next batch's scheduling and launch under overlap. The two forward series (`forward_pass_duration_seconds`, `decode_step_latency_seconds`) are device-measured. Splitting them means neither name lies.

**3. PP gating** now matches FPM exactly — `attn_tp_rank == 0 and pp_rank == pp_size - 1` — on both the emission and the timestamp stamp. `pp_size == 1` is unchanged. I checked the failure mode in the other direction too: `_pp_process_batch_result` is not rank-gated, so the final stage does reach `process_batch_result` and this does not swing from N samples to zero. The docs now also state that with `--pp-size` the value is the *final stage's* forward, not full-model latency — otherwise the number is easy to misread under PP.

**Tests.** The overlap-ordering regression test runs the same simulated step twice, with 0 ms and 50 ms of next-batch work after the forward, and asserts the forward observation stays 10 ms while only schedule-to-result grows. Reverting the production files makes it fail on the *value* (`0.020 != 0.010`), and three PP subcases fail `1 != 0` — so it regresses for the right reason rather than on a missing attribute. Also added tests that device time is not carried into the next batch, that the two series never leak into each other, and that the Prometheus drain still feeds FPM (`DeviceTimer._report()` fans out to all reporters; if that ever became single-subscriber FPM would silently read zero). Thanks for adding these metrics. Reading `c30a6f0`, I think `decode_step_latency_seconds` doesn't see prefill stalls when `--enable-mixed-chunk` is off, which is the default.

`_forward_pass_composition` counts decode requests as `len(batch.decoding_reqs)`, and `decoding_reqs` is set only when `mix_with_running` merges the running batch into the prefill batch. Without mixed chunk, `get_next_batch_to_run` runs the prefill batch first and the running decode batch waits a whole step. That step is recorded as `forward_pass_duration_seconds{phase="prefill_only", decode_reqs_bucket="0"}` and never reaches `decode_step_latency_seconds`.

So the check in the docs (`mixed` p99 against `decode_only` p99) shows no interference while prefill is stalling streams. Mixed chunk is off by default on current `main`, and some configurations (diffusion LLMs, HiSparse, several speculative decoding setups) turn it off or reject it, so enabling it doesn't always work around this.

I measured this client-side with Qwen3-8B on one H100, SGLang v0.5.21, defaults (mixed chunk off, chunked prefill 8,192). The load was 8 short streaming requests/s, alone and then with one 3,118-token prompt per second added:

| | alone | with long prompts |
|---|---|---|
| inter-token gaps over 50 ms, per minute | 27 | 361 |
| replies with such a gap | 5% | 48% |
| p99 inter-token gap | 20 ms | 23 ms |
| p99.9 inter-token gap | 33 ms | 84 ms |
| longest gap | 108 ms | 255 ms |

724 of the 739 gaps over 30 ms began within 0.15 s of a long prompt arriving. Each long prompt fits in one 8,192-token chunk, so these gaps are prefill-only steps (one, or a few back to back) while the decode batch waits.

A possible fix: `prefill_stats` already carries `num_running_reqs` for the batch that waits. For an extend pass without `decoding_reqs`, record the pass in `decode_step_latency_seconds` under its own phase, e.g. `phase="prefill_blocking"`, with `decode_reqs_bucket` from that count. The docs would then compare `mixed|prefill_blocking` against `decode_only`. I'm happy to send this as a commit on your branch or as a follow-up PR, whichever you prefer.
